result.markdown: --- title: "Week 07: Variability & Model Fit with JAMOVI" subtitle: "Date: October 8, 2026" footer: "[course-website](https://dharaden.github.io/psyc640/)" logo: "images/640_hex.png" format: revealjs: theme: [default, brand, clean.scss] multiplex: false transition: fade slide-number: true incremental: false chalkboard: true overview: false scrollable: true code-line-numbers: true editor: visual execute: echo: true freeze: auto --- ## Today... **How good is this model, actually?** - Where the variance goes: $SS_{total} = SS_{model} + SS_{residual}$ - R², one more time — and what it is *not* - The typical miss, in real units - The F test as a ratio - Why R² can only go **up**, and what to use instead - 👀 A sneak peek at two predictors ::: callout-note This is the **JAMOVI** version. Same data, same numbers as the R deck. JAMOVI is genuinely *better* than base R at one thing today — comparing nested models — so stick around for Part 3. ::: ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ## Our data: the ASAP study 😴 400 adolescents, measured on sleep, stress, and mood. Download the ASAP data (.csv) > ☰ **Menu → Open → Browse →** `asap_data.csv` > **Analyses → Exploration → Descriptives** · `T1_SleepDur`, `T1_PeerStress`, `T1_AcadStress`, `T1_Dep` | Variable | N | Mean | SD | |-------------------|-------------------|-------------------|-------------------| | `T1_SleepDur` (hours) | 400 | 9.45 | 1.00 | | `T1_PeerStress` | 400 | 7.93 | 1.77 | | `T1_AcadStress` | 400 | 5.02 | 1.83 | | `T1_Dep` | 400 | 9.84 | **2.15** | > **Research question:** Does how long adolescents sleep predict depressive symptoms? # Part 1: Where Does the Variance Go? ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ## Start with the dumbest possible model Suppose you had **no predictor at all**. What is your best guess for anyone's depression score? . . . The **mean**: 9.84. That's it. That's the model. . . . How wrong is that model? Add up every squared miss: $$SS_{total} = \sum(Y_i - \bar{Y})^2 = 1840.5$$ This is the **total variability** we are trying to account for. Everything from here is about shrinking it. ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ## Now add a predictor > **Analyses → Regression → Linear Regression** > > Dependent Variable: `T1_Dep` · **Covariates:** `T1_SleepDur` > > Model Fit: tick **R²**, **Adjusted R²**, **RMSE**, **Overall Model Test** > > Model Coefficients: tick **Omnibus ANOVA Test** | Predictor | Estimate | SE | t | p | |-------------|-------------|-------------|-------------|-------------| | Intercept | 15.031 | 0.985 | 15.26 | \< .001 | | T1_SleepDur | **−0.549** | 0.104 | **−5.30** | **\< .001** | Each additional hour of sleep is associated with **0.55 fewer** points of depression. But today's question is: **how much better is this line than the mean?** ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ## Three distances, one observation For any single adolescent: ::::: columns ::: {.column width="50%"} $$\underbrace{Y_i - \bar{Y}}_{\text{total}} = \underbrace{\hat{Y_i} - \bar{Y}}_{\text{model}} + \underbrace{Y_i - \hat{Y_i}}_{\text{residual}}$$ ::: ::: {.column width="50%"} - **Total**: how far this person is from the overall mean - **Model**: how far the *line* moved them from the mean - **Residual**: how far the line still missed ::: ::::: . . . Square them, add them up across all 400 people, and the same decomposition holds: $$SS_{total} = SS_{model} + SS_{residual}$$ ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ## See it in the numbers The **Omnibus ANOVA Test** table you just ticked: | Term | Sum of Squares | df | Mean Square | F | p | |------------|------------|------------|------------|------------|------------| | T1_SleepDur | **121.2** | 1 | 121.2 | 28.05 | \< .001 | | Residuals | **1719.4** | 398 | 4.32 | | | ::: incremental - $SS_{model}$ = **121.2** — variability the line accounts for - $SS_{residual}$ = **1719.4** — variability it does not - Together: 121.2 + 1719.4 = **1840.5** = $SS_{total}$ ✅ ::: ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ## R² is just a share $$R^2 = \frac{SS_{model}}{SS_{total}} = \frac{121.2}{1840.5} = .066$$ **Model Fit Measures** | R | R² | Adjusted R² | RMSE | |------------------|------------------|------------------|------------------| | 0.257 | **0.0658** | 0.0635 | 2.073 | . . . **6.6%** of the variability in depression is accounted for by sleep duration. Which means **93.4% is not**. Both halves of that sentence are the finding. ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ## Small R², strong evidence ::::: columns ::: {.column width="50%"} **R² = .066** Sleep duration tells us very little about any individual adolescent's depression. ::: ::: {.column width="50%"} **p \< .001** With n = 400, we are confident the slope is not zero. ::: ::::: . . . ::: callout-important These are answers to **different questions**. "Is there an effect?" and "how much does it explain?" are not the same, and a p-value only answers the first. ::: . . . This is normal in psychology. Behavior has many causes; one predictor rarely owns much of the variance. # Part 2: Fit in Real Units ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ## R² is unitless. That's a problem. ".066" does not tell you whether this model is useful for a clinician. . . . **RMSE** does. It is roughly the size of a typical miss, in the units of the outcome: $$RMSE \approx \sqrt{\frac{SS_{residual}}{n}} = \sqrt{\frac{1719.4}{400}} = 2.07$$ ::: callout-note JAMOVI's RMSE divides by *n*; R's "residual standard error" divides by the degrees of freedom (2.08 here). Same idea, trivially different arithmetic — don't let the two labels confuse you. ::: ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ## The comparison that matters ::: incremental - Guess the **mean** for everyone → you are off by about **2.15** points on average - Use the **model** → you are off by about **2.07** points ::: . . . We bought ourselves about **0.08 points** of accuracy. . . . ::: callout-tip That is the honest way to describe a small R² to a non-statistician: *not* "6.6% of variance," which means nothing to most people, but "knowing how long a teenager slept barely improves our guess about their mood." ::: ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ## The F test is a ratio $$F = \frac{MS_{model}}{MS_{residual}} = \frac{121.2}{4.32} = 28.05$$ **Overall Model Test** | F | df1 | df2 | p | |------------------|------------------|------------------|------------------| | **28.05** | 1 | 398 | \< .001 | ::: incremental - If the model explained **nothing**, F would hover around 1 - With one predictor, $F = t^2$: $(-5.30)^2 = 28.05$ ✅ — the same test again ::: # Part 3: Adding Predictors 👀 ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ## JAMOVI's best trick: Model Builder > **Linear Regression → Model Builder** > > **Block 1:** `T1_SleepDur` > > Click **+ Add New Block** → **Block 2:** `T1_PeerStress` . . . Now tick **Model Comparisons** under Model Fit. JAMOVI will fit *both* models and test the difference between them — which is exactly the question "did peer stress earn its place?" ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ## Does peer stress help? **Model Comparisons** | Comparison | ΔR² | F | df1 | df2 | p | |------------|------------|------------|------------|------------|------------| | Model 1 − Model 2 | **0.027** | 11.78 | 1 | 397 | **\< .001** | **Model Fit Measures** | Model | R² | Adjusted R² | RMSE | |------------------|------------------|------------------|------------------| | 1. Sleep only | .0658 | .0635 | 2.073 | | 2. \+ peer stress | **.0928** | **.0882** | **2.043** | ::: incremental - $\Delta R^2$ = **.027** — peer stress accounts for 2.7% *beyond* sleep - The typical miss dropped from 2.073 to 2.043 ::: ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ## Now let's add something useless > **+ Add New Block** → **Block 3:** `T1_AcadStress` | Predictor | Estimate | SE | t | p | |-------------|-------------|-------------|-------------|-------------| | T1_AcadStress | **−0.007** | 0.057 | −0.12 | **0.902** | Academic stress is as close to nothing as you will ever see. ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ## Watch what R² does | Model | R² | Adjusted R² | RMSE | |------------------|------------------|------------------|------------------| | 1. Sleep only | .0658 | .0635 | 2.073 | | 2. \+ peer stress | .0928 | .0882 | 2.043 | | 3. \+ academic stress | **.0928** | **.0859** ⬇️ | 2.043 | ::: incremental - R² **did not go down** — it never can - Adjusted R² **did** - And Model Comparisons reports the block as non-significant, *p* = .90 ::: ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ## Why R² can only climb Adding a predictor gives the model one more knob to turn. At worst the coefficient sits near zero and fit stays the same; usually it catches a sliver of noise and R² ticks up. . . . $$R^2_{adj} = 1 - (1 - R^2)\frac{n - 1}{n - k - 1}$$ Every predictor $k$ costs you something. Adjusted R² only rises if the new variable earns its place. ::: callout-important **R² is not a model-selection tool.** The biggest R² always belongs to the model with the most predictors. Week 11 gives us honest ways to compare models — and JAMOVI's Model Comparisons table is the first one. ::: ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ## JAMOVI ↔ R cheat sheet | What you want | JAMOVI | R | |------------------------|------------------------|------------------------| | R², adjusted R² | Model Fit Measures | `glance(fit)` | | Typical miss | Model Fit → **RMSE** | `glance(fit)$sigma` | | Sums of squares | Model Coefficients → **Omnibus ANOVA Test** | `anova(fit)` | | Overall F | Model Fit → Overall Model Test | `glance(fit)$statistic` | | Compare nested models | **Model Builder** blocks + Model Comparisons | `anova(fit1, fit2)` | | ΔR² | Model Comparisons table | subtract two `glance()` rows | ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ## ⏱️ One last thing: look at the residuals {background-color="#EFE6F7"} We spent all day computing $SS_{residual}$. Let's actually **look** at the residuals instead of just squaring them. > **Linear Regression → Assumption Checks** > > Tick **Residual plots** JAMOVI gives you residuals against fitted values (plus a Q-Q plot). For the ASAP model it is a shapeless cloud centered on zero — which is what "nothing obviously wrong" looks like. ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ## What you are glancing for ::: {.cell} ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](lec-07_fit_JAMOVI_files/figure-revealjs/unnamed-chunk-1-1.png){width=960} ::: ::: ::: incremental - **Curve** → the line is the wrong shape for these data - **Funnel** → the model is more wrong for some people than others - **Strange point** → one observation may be running the whole model (remember the 1,000-books reader?) ::: . . . ::: callout-note That is the entire diagnostic toolkit for now: **tick the box, look for a pattern.** Week 10 turns each of these into a named assumption with a proper test. For the midterm, the glance is enough. ::: ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ## 🛠️ Activity: Does the Algorithm Know What a Hit Is? ::: callout-tip **Week 7 Exercises** · \~45 min · Pairs ::: Spotify data: 952 popular songs, with danceability, energy, valence, acousticness — and streams. - Four audio features together explain about **1%** of streams - One boring variable explains **62%** - You will find it, and then explain why the fancy features lost [Open the activity](../class-activities/wk7_fit.html){.button target="_blank"} ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ## ✍️ Wrap-Up Finish these at the bottom of your activity file: 1. In one sentence, explain R² to someone who has never taken statistics. 2. Why can a predictor be statistically significant and still barely improve a model? 3. One thing that is still muddy → journal. ------------------------------------------------------------------------ ## For next time 📋 **Lab 8 — How Good Is This Model?**, due **Tuesday 10/13 at 11:59pm** ::: callout-warning **10/13 is during Fall Break.** The lab is submitted online as usual — nothing to hand in physically, and no class that Monday or Tuesday. ::: - Model fit on a real anxiety dataset, in the units people care about - Ends with a **sneak peek**: one predictor that looks useless alone, and what happens when you add a second 📖 Chapter 10 — ROS (for next week's multiple regression) ::: callout-important ## 📂 Midterm Project — posted today The [**Midterm Project**](../labs/midterm-project.html) is up on the website now. **Due Tuesday, 10/27 at 11:59pm.** It is worth 200 points (20% of your grade). - **Parts 1-5 use only what you already know** - cleaning, scoring, describing, one-predictor models. You can start this weekend. - **Part 6 needs multiple regression**, which is next class (10/15). - You pick your own research question. Read the whole thing before you leave today. No lab is due in Weeks 9 or 10, so that time is yours for the project. :::

<script>
  // htmlwidgets need to know to resize themselves when slides are shown/hidden.
  // Fire the "slideenter" event (handled by htmlwidgets.js) when the current
  // slide changes (different for each slide format).
  (function () {
    // dispatch for htmlwidgets
    function fireSlideEnter() {
      const event = window.document.createEvent("Event");
      event.initEvent("slideenter", true, true);
      window.document.dispatchEvent(event);
    }

    function fireSlideChanged(previousSlide, currentSlide) {
      fireSlideEnter();

      // dispatch for shiny
      if (window.jQuery) {
        if (previousSlide) {
          window.jQuery(previousSlide).trigger("hidden");
        }
        if (currentSlide) {
          window.jQuery(currentSlide).trigger("shown");
        }
      }
    }

    // hookup for slidy
    if (window.w3c_slidy) {
      window.w3c_slidy.add_observer(function (slide_num) {
        // slide_num starts at position 1
        fireSlideChanged(null, w3c_slidy.slides[slide_num - 1]);
      });
    }

  })();
</script>
